lead: An audiometer is a calibrated tone generator with headphones. It sends a pure tone of known frequency and known level to one ear, and the tester finds the softest level the person hears. That level is the hearing threshold. The result is plotted as hearing level in dB HL against frequency, giving an audiogram. Clinics use it to detect hearing loss, to fit hearing aids, and to screen workers exposed to loud machinery or schoolchildren. This chapter covers pure-tone audiometry and a short look at speech audiometry.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, Bioelectric Signals, Electrodes and Recorders (tone generator, attenuator and output stage reuse amplifier and filter ideas), and see 6.4 for current paths through the body and 6.5 for equipment safety.

sections.h3: Air conduction, bone conduction and the audiogram

blocks.text: A pure-tone audiometer has an oscillator, a frequency selector, an attenuator and an earphone. The oscillator makes a sine wave from 125 Hz to 8 kHz. The attenuator sets the level in 5 dB steps. The earphone delivers the tone to one ear. Air conduction tests the whole path: outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.

Bone conduction uses a small vibrator pressed on the mastoid bone behind the ear. The sound reaches the inner ear through the skull and skips the outer and middle ear. Comparing air and bone thresholds separates conductive loss (outer or middle ear) from sensorineural loss (inner ear or nerve).

The result is an audiogram. Frequency is on the horizontal axis from 125 Hz to 8 kHz. Hearing level is on the vertical axis in dB HL, marked 0 to 100; 0 is normal and larger numbers mean worse hearing. In the figure, a normal ear sits at 0 dB HL at every frequency. The patient hears 20 dB HL at 250 Hz, 35 dB at 500 Hz, 45 dB at 1 kHz, 55 dB at 2 kHz and 60 dB at 4 kHz.

Hearing level uses a reference pressure that changes with frequency. At 1 kHz, 0 dB HL is 20 µPa, about the quietest tone a normal young ear can hear. At other frequencies the reference is different, so 0 dB HL is not the same sound pressure level (SPL) everywhere.

blocks.where: L<sub>HL</sub> is hearing level in dB HL; p is the sound pressure at the ear; p<sub>ref</sub>(f) is the normal threshold pressure at frequency f; at 1 kHz p<sub>ref</sub> = 20 µPa.

blocks.text: The Hughson-Westlake method is a staircase. It finds the lowest level heard, not the first level heard.

items: Explain the test and place the headphones. Test the better ear first.
Start at 1 kHz with a tone at 30 dB HL for about one second.
If the tone is heard, drop by 10 dB and repeat.
After a miss, raise by 5 dB and repeat.
The threshold is the lowest level heard on two of three ascending runs.

blocks.text: Masking stops the non-test ear from hearing the tone by bone conduction. Feed narrow-band noise, centred on the test frequency, to the non-test ear. Mask when the air-bone gap is large or when the tone could cross the skull. Masking noise goes to the non-test ear, never the test ear.

Speech audiometry asks what the ear does with words, not just tones. The speech reception threshold (SRT) is the level at which the person repeats half of a list of two-syllable words correctly. Some syllabi call this speech reception threshold testing. SRT should agree with the pure-tone average of 500 Hz, 1 kHz and 2 kHz within about 10 dB. A word recognition score uses a fixed list at a comfortable level and reports the percentage repeated correctly.

Calibration keeps the numbers honest. A coupler and a sound-level meter set the reference equivalent threshold sound pressure level at each frequency for the earphone model. A daily biological check on a known normal ear catches drift. The 1 kHz reference of 20 µPa is the anchor for the dB HL scale.

figure.caption: Hearing level against frequency. The flat line at 0 dB HL marks normal hearing; the patient curve rises from 20 dB at 250 Hz to 60 dB at 4000 Hz, so higher numbers mean quieter tones are missed.

spec.aria: Hearing level against frequency: a flat line at 0 dB HL for normal ears and a patient curve rising from 20 dB at 250 Hz to 60 dB at 4000 Hz.

examples.question: A pure-tone audiometer is calibrated so that 0 dB HL at 1 kHz equals a sound pressure of 20 µPa. A patient hears the 1 kHz tone only when the dial is at 60 dB HL. What pressure reached the ear?
steps: Write the hearing-level formula: L = 20 log<sub>10</sub>(p / p<sub>0</sub>).
Put L = 60 dB and p<sub>0</sub> = 20 µPa.
examples.answer: The pressure reached the ear is 20 mPa, which is one thousand times the 20 µPa reference.
examples.check:
L = 60
p0 = 20e-6
ratio = 10 ** (L / 20)
p = p0 * ratio
print(ratio)
print(p * 1000)

traps: dB HL is not dB SPL. A reading of 40 dB HL means 40 dB above the normal threshold at that frequency, not a fixed pressure, because the reference pressure changes with frequency.
Air conduction and bone conduction are not two names for the same test. Bone conduction skips the outer and middle ear, so an air-bone gap points to a conductive component.
Masking noise is delivered to the non-test ear. Sending it to the test ear raises the threshold and gives a false reading.
The Hughson-Westlake rule is 10 dB down after a heard tone and 5 dB up after a miss. Reversing these steps gives the wrong threshold.
SRT and the word recognition score are different numbers. SRT is the 50% speech level; the word score is a percentage at a chosen comfortable level.

quiz.q: What does 0 dB HL mean at 1 kHz?
quiz.a: It is the normal hearing threshold at 1 kHz, set at a sound pressure of 20 µPa.

quiz.q: Why does an audiogram use dB HL instead of dB SPL?
quiz.a: dB HL compares the patient with the normal threshold at each frequency. The reference pressure changes with frequency, so equal dB HL means equal distance above normal hearing, not equal pressure.

quiz.q: A patient hears a 1 kHz tone at 40 dB HL. Using p<sub>ref</sub> = 20 µPa, find the pressure at the ear.
quiz.a: L = 20 log<sub>10</sub>(p/p<sub>0</sub>), so p/p<sub>0</sub> = 10<sup>(40/20)</sup> = 100. p = 20 µPa × 100 = 2000 µPa = 2 mPa.

quiz.q: In a Hughson-Westlake run, the patient hears 40 dB HL. What is the next level if the response continues to follow the staircase?
quiz.a: After a heard tone, drop 10 dB: the next level is 30 dB HL. If 30 dB is missed, raise 5 dB to 35 dB HL.

quiz.q: At 1 kHz, air conduction is 50 dB HL and bone conduction is 20 dB HL. What does this pattern suggest?
quiz.a: There is a 30 dB air-bone gap. Bone conduction is near normal at 20 dB HL, so the loss is mostly conductive, coming from the outer or middle ear rather than the inner ear or nerve.

quiz.q: Why is narrow-band noise used for masking rather than a pure tone?
quiz.a: Narrow-band noise around the test frequency masks the non-test ear without adding a second pure tone that the patient could confuse with the test tone.

quiz.q: Name the two transducers used in pure-tone audiometry and what each tests.
quiz.a: An earphone tests air conduction through the outer, middle and inner ear. A bone vibrator on the mastoid tests bone conduction through the skull to the inner ear.

beyond: Not for the exam. Portable audiometers now run on a phone or a tablet with calibrated earphones, and tele-audiology sends the audiogram to a distant clinic. Automated audiometry uses the same Hughson-Westlake staircase without a tester. Research links audiogram shape to noise exposure, medicines that damage the ear, and ageing. Search for smartphone audiometry, otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response to see the next layer of hearing tests.
